name: Bandjoun (Djo)
autonymMeaning: “those who buy”, those who have money
overview: The Djo of Bandjoun form a large chiefdom of the West, descended from peoples who came from Ŋwa (Haut-Nkam), Baleng and the Bamoun country. Kingship, brotherhoods and the skull cult structure society; coffee, trade and crafts (forging, basketry, sculpture) sustain it, and the Msəm Tódjom festival brings the community together in odd-numbered years.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, formed from the union of peoples of diverse origins; all speak the language of Bandjoun, which is not spoken elsewhere in this form.
Mostly indigenous, he takes wives among the Eton, in Gabon, in the North, in Baham or Bayangam, but tends rather towards endogamy.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land linked to the sacred.
Having come from Ŋwa (Haut-Nkam), Baleng and the Bamoun country, the Djo still return there for ceremonies.
Like other Grassfields peoples, they fought wars over land: a trench (tsʉ́) still marks the border with Bayangam.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship, brotherhoods, social classes and modern administration organise society; decisions are made by consensus after debate, at the chiefdom or in the brotherhoods.
Interactions are not hierarchical, but young people follow rules when addressing nobles, whose rights must be respected.
In the traditional lodges, men and women are separated.
Relations with neighbours, after ancient battles, are good today.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband.

A boy becomes a man at around twenty, when he builds his hut and takes a wife; it is said that a girl asserts herself as a woman when she starts to stand up to her mother. Marriages around the age of twenty.
Steps: meeting, “knocking at the door” (official request), bride price.

Bride price: oil, pork in a basket (the new family being founded), goat, wrappers (keepsake of the marriage), pistachio dish prepared by the young woman's family to honour the husband's family, kola and white wine that seal the union for ever.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Skull cult: the skulls of deserving ancestors are kept; the successor honours them on fixed days, in joy as in sorrow.
Sacred places in each large compound and for the whole community, visited by the chief: tǎmnɔk near the enieg of Bandjoun, Tókɔ at Djá'gɛ, marked by plants.
The child is a gift obtained from God through the intercession of the forebears, a bond between families and between the living and God.
A distinction is made between the dead, who are quickly forgotten, and the ancestors, who are asked to intercede with God.
Taboos: incest, theft, infidelity. The man does not covet another's wife; the woman has a day without work in the fields and does not eat gizzard; children do not eat eggs.
Divination and clairvoyance, practised mostly by men.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: trade, coffee, traditional livestock rearing, motorbike taxi. Women: fieldwork.
The land belongs to the men; it is obtained by inheritance or purchase.
Ancestral crafts: forging (knives, machetes, axes), basketry (mats, hampers, baskets), wood carving.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Boubou and traditional hat after the chair ceremony; ndop outfit (zhu ndop) for the nobility and for mourning; wrapper in all its forms.
Traditional medicine remains alive.
Beauty: robustness for men, hips for women.
Courtship: the man comes back from the market with meat for a woman; the woman prepares her husband's favourite dish.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances: mewup (men; small and large drum, balafons, rattles), làlì (sacred men's dance; drums, balafon, drum), métō' (women, rattles on the ankles), mesu (dance of the princesses), tsó (sacred and secret dance, rarely performed).
Festival: the great Msəm Tódjom festival, in odd-numbered years in November.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Like the other neighbouring communities, the Djo traditionally did not know divorce.

sections.title: The names
items: tá is placed before a man's name, djui or má before a woman's name.
It is the husband's father who names the child; one very rarely changes names (illness, bad luck), once at most.
Men are called by their titles and women by their husband's title; people of lower rank add tá before the title of notability.
The founding ancestor is called Tódzɔm.

lessons.title: Who are the Bandjoun (Djo)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bandjoun (Djo) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Bandjoun (Djo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bandjoun (Djo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bandjoun (Djo) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bandjoun (Djo) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bandjoun (Djo) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, formed from the union of peoples of diverse origins; all speak the language of Bandjoun, which is not spoken elsewhere in this form. • Mostly indigenous, it takes wives from among the Eton, in Gabon, in the North, at Baham or at Bayangam, but tends rather towards endogamy. • Ancestral land linked to the sacred. • Having come from Ŋwa (Haut-Nkam), from Baleng and from the Bamoun country, the Djo still return there for ceremonies.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Djo of Bandjoun form a large chiefdom of the West, descended from peoples who came from Ŋwa (Haut-Nkam), Baleng and the Bamoun country. Kingship, brotherhoods and the skull cult structure society; coffee, trade and crafts (forging, basketry, sculpture) sustain it, and the Msəm Tódjom festival brings the community together in odd-numbered years.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bandjoun (Djo) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

objectives: Linking food to the living environment

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bandjoun (Djo), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bandjoun (Djo), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bandjoun (Djo).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: couscous and nkwi greens (msè pfʉ), taro in yellow sauce, pounded banana with black beans, pistachio dishes. • Drinks: palm wine. • Men: trade, coffee, traditional livestock rearing, motorbike taxi. Women: fieldwork.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bandjoun (Djo) mainly eat msè pfʉ, taro in yellow sauce, pounded banana with black beans, pistachio-seed dishes. Traditional drinks: palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.instruction: Among the Bandjoun (Djo), traditional dances (mewup, métō', mesu) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drums, balafons, rattles, drum. Festival(s): Msəm Tódjom.

lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bandjoun (Djo)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bandjoun (Djo), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bandjoun (Djo). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bandjoun (Djo)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bandjoun (Djo), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bandjoun (Djo). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bandjoun (Djo), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bandjoun (Djo). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Skull worship: those of deserving ancestors are kept; the successor honours them on fixed days, in joy and in sorrow. • Sacred places in each large compound and for the whole community, visited by the chief: tǎmnɔk near the enieg of Bandjoun, Tókɔ at Djá'gɛ, marked by plants. • The child is a gift obtained from God through the intercession of the ancestors, a bond between families and between the living and God. • A distinction is made between the dead who are quickly forgotten and the ancestors, whom people pray to intercede with God. • Taboos: incest, theft, infidelity. A man does not covet another's wife; a woman has a day without work in the fields and does not eat gizzard; children do not eat eggs.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Skull cult: the skulls of deserving ancestors are kept; the successor honours them on fixed days, in joy as in sorrow. Sacred places in each large compound and for the whole community, visited by the chief: tǎmnɔk near the enieg of Bandjoun, Tókɔ at Djá'gɛ, marked by plants.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bandjoun (Djo) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ghomala'
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bandjoun (Djo) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bandjoun (Djo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bandjoun (Djo) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bandjoun (Djo) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Ghomala'. • Greeting formulae: Ŋgə t∫s’te = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Ǒ ti jú lᾁ = morning greeting (one person); Pǒ ti jɔ́ lᾁ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ya:m, Ya pʉᾁ, ya tá, Ya pʉᾁ, Ya tô. • The founding ancestor is called Tódzɔm. • Like the other neighbouring communities, the Djo traditionally did not know divorce.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ghomala' are the first steps towards communicating with the Bandjoun (Djo). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
